claim: The central helix (CH) of complexin directly binds the ternary SNARE complex.
source: Its highly conserved central helix (CH) directly binds the ternary SNARE complex and is required for all known CPX functions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of complexin.

claim: The central helix (CH) is required for all known complexin functions.
source: Its highly conserved central helix (CH) directly binds the ternary SNARE complex and is required for all known CPX functions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: The accessory helix (AH) is not conserved in primary sequence.
source: The adjacent accessory helix (AH) is not conserved despite also playing an important role in CPX function, and numerous models for its mechanism have been proposed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1B showing only 20% identity between mammals and nematodes.

claim: The accessory helix (AH) plays an important role in complexin function.
source: The adjacent accessory helix (AH) is not conserved despite also playing an important role in CPX function, and numerous models for its mechanism have been proposed.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through functional assays in the manuscript.

claim: The mouse AH fully restored function when substituted into worm CPX.
source: The mouse AH fully restored function when substituted into worm CPX suggesting its mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3B-D showing rescue of spontaneous fusion and aldicarb sensitivity.

claim: The mechanism of the accessory helix is evolutionarily conserved.
source: The mouse AH fully restored function when substituted into worm CPX suggesting its mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional rescue experiments with mouse AH in worm CPX.

claim: CPX inhibitory function was impaired when helix propagation into the CH was disrupted.
source: CPX inhibitory function was impaired when helix propagation into the CH was disrupted whereas replacing the AH with a non-native helical sequence restored CPX function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the GG insertion experiment in Figure 5E.

claim: Replacing the AH with a non-native helical sequence restored CPX function.
source: CPX inhibitory function was impaired when helix propagation into the CH was disrupted whereas replacing the AH with a non-native helical sequence restored CPX function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the 7-turn EAAK helix substitution in Figure 6.

claim: The AH operates by stabilizing CH secondary structure rather than through protein or lipid interactions.
source: We propose that the AH operates by stabilizing CH secondary structure rather than through protein or lipid interactions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed in the abstract based on the experimental results.

claim: Genetic ablation of complexin profoundly impacts neurotransmitter release in all synaptic preparations studied to date.
source: Complexin is another essential SNARE-binding protein, and genetic ablation of complexin profoundly impacts neurotransmitter release and its regulation in all synaptic preparations studied to date (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Xue et al., 2008; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2013; Vaithianathan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Deletion of the two broadly expressed mammalian complexin isoforms (mCpx1/2) is lethal.
source: Mammals possess four isoforms of complexin, and deletion of the two broadly expressed isoforms (mCpx1/2) is lethal (Reim et al., 2001; Xue et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The central helix (CH) domain is broadly conserved among metazoa.
source: This small cytoplasmic protein possesses an alpha-helical SNARE-binding domain known as the central helix (CH), which is broadly conserved among metazoa (Pabst et al., 2000; Reim et al., 2001; Bracher et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2002; Brose, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The CH domain of mCpx1 is flanked on its N-terminus by a stable alpha helix called the accessory helix (AH).
source: The CH domain of mCpx1 is flanked on its N-terminus by a stable alpha helix called the accessory helix (AH) (Pabst et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002), and this domain has subsequently been shown to play an inhibitory role in mammalian, fly, and nematode synapses (Xue et al., 2007, 2009; Yang et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The AH domain plays an inhibitory role in mammalian, fly, and nematode synapses.
source: The CH domain of mCpx1 is flanked on its N-terminus by a stable alpha helix called the accessory helix (AH) (Pabst et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002), and this domain has subsequently been shown to play an inhibitory role in mammalian, fly, and nematode synapses (Xue et al., 2007, 2009; Yang et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: The primary sequence of the AH domain is poorly conserved.
source: However, the primary sequence of the AH domain is poorly conserved, and its secondary structure has only been investigated in rodent complexin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1B.

claim: The secondary structure of the AH has only been investigated in rodent complexin.
source: However, the primary sequence of the AH domain is poorly conserved, and its secondary structure has only been investigated in rodent complexin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: The central helix of mouse complexin binds tightly to the assembled SNARE bundle.
source: A region of the alpha helical domain of mouse complexin binds tightly to the assembled SNARE bundle (Figure 1A), positioned in the groove formed by synaptobrevin and syntaxin (Bracher et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The central helix is positioned in the groove formed by synaptobrevin and syntaxin.
source: A region of the alpha helical domain of mouse complexin binds tightly to the assembled SNARE bundle (Figure 1A), positioned in the groove formed by synaptobrevin and syntaxin (Bracher et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The central helix is deeply conserved across phylogeny with 76% identity between mammals and nematodes.
source: This so-called 'central helix' (CH) is deeply conserved across phylogeny (76% identity between mammals and nematodes), whereas the adjacent helical sequence corresponding to the mouse accessory helix (AH) is much more heterogeneous, with only 20% identity between mammals and nematodes based on the 18 residues N-terminal to CH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B sequence alignment.

claim: The accessory helix has only 20% identity between mammals and nematodes.
source: This so-called 'central helix' (CH) is deeply conserved across phylogeny (76% identity between mammals and nematodes), whereas the adjacent helical sequence corresponding to the mouse accessory helix (AH) is much more heterogeneous, with only 20% identity between mammals and nematodes based on the 18 residues N-terminal to CH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Worm complexin CPX-1 possesses a highly stable helical region including 30 residues between P37 and G66.
source: Computational predictions based on amino acid sequence indicated a highly stable helical region including 30 residues between P37 and G66 encompassing the AH and half of the CH domain (Figure 1C,D) (Munoz and Serrano, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C,D with computational predictions.

claim: The helical region of worm CPX-1 was confirmed by solution-state NMR spectroscopy.
source: This domain was confirmed to be helical by solution-state NMR spectroscopy on recombinant full-length worm CPX-1 (Snead et al., 2014) as well as on a truncated version lacking its C-terminal domain (Figure 1C,D), validating the computational predictions for this protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The stable helical structure of the AH domain is predicted to be deeply conserved across phylogeny.
source: The stable helical structure of the AH domain is predicted to be deeply conserved across phylogeny based on the analysis of complexin sequences in 16 diverse metazoan species from seven phyla ranging from Trychoplax to human (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: Both mouse and worm complexin possess a stable alpha helical domain N-terminal to the CH despite sharing little sequence homology.
source: Thus both mouse and worm complexin possess a stable alpha helical domain N-terminal to the CH despite sharing little sequence homology, and this is likely to be a universal feature of complexin.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: A stable alpha helical domain N-terminal to the CH is likely to be a universal feature of complexin.
source: Thus both mouse and worm complexin possess a stable alpha helical domain N-terminal to the CH despite sharing little sequence homology, and this is likely to be a universal feature of complexin.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation analysis across 16 species.

claim: Loss of CPX-1 caused a 12-fold increase in the rate of spontaneous fusion in the absence of external calcium at cholinergic NMJs.
source: Loss of CPX-1 caused a 12-fold increase in the rate of spontaneous fusion in the absence of external calcium at cholinergic NMJs (Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Wragg et al., 2013) (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations and shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Rescue with full-length CPX-1 completely restored the basal synaptic vesicle fusion rate.
source: Rescue with full-length CPX-1 completely restored the basal synaptic vesicle (SV) fusion rate (3.3 ± 0.9 Hz for wild type, 2.7 ± 0.5 Hz for FL rescue) whereas rescue with the ΔAHshort variant only partially reversed the increased rate of spontaneous fusion (39.8 ± 6.2 Hz for cpx-1, 20.8 ± 5.6 Hz for ΔAHshort rescue).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific numerical data.

claim: Rescue with the ΔAHshort variant only partially reversed the increased rate of spontaneous fusion.
source: Rescue with full-length CPX-1 completely restored the basal synaptic vesicle (SV) fusion rate (3.3 ± 0.9 Hz for wild type, 2.7 ± 0.5 Hz for FL rescue) whereas rescue with the ΔAHshort variant only partially reversed the increased rate of spontaneous fusion (39.8 ± 6.2 Hz for cpx-1, 20.8 ± 5.6 Hz for ΔAHshort rescue).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific numerical data.

claim: CPX-1 retained a limited ability to inhibit fusion in the absence of the AH domain.
source: Thus CPX-1 retained a limited ability to inhibit fusion in the absence of the AH domain.
evidence: This is concluded from the partial rescue observed with ΔAHshort.

claim: The muscle miniature EPSC amplitude was unaffected by CPX-1 mutations.
source: In all cases, the muscle miniature EPSC amplitude was unaffected (Figure 2D), consistent with the neuronal expression of CPX-1 in C. elegans (Martin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: cpx-1 mutants exposed to aldicarb paralyzed more rapidly than wild-type animals.
source: cpx-1 mutants exposed to the cholinesterase inhibitor aldicarb paralyzed more rapidly than wild-type animals (Figure 2E,F) as described previously (Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Wragg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations and shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Rescue with ΔAHshort or ΔAHlong only partially restored wild-type aldicarb sensitivity.
source: Consistent with the NMJ recordings, rescue with ΔAHshort or ΔAHlong only partially restored wild-type sensitivity whereas full-length CPX-1 completely rescued aldicarb sensitivity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Full-length CPX-1 completely rescued aldicarb sensitivity.
source: Consistent with the NMJ recordings, rescue with ΔAHshort or ΔAHlong only partially restored wild-type sensitivity whereas full-length CPX-1 completely rescued aldicarb sensitivity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The helix-breaking proline in position 37 is shared by all published nematode genomes.
source: The helix-breaking proline in position 37 is shared by all of the published nematode genomes, so the short AH domain is a common feature of this phylum.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: Deletion of proline 37 does not impair CPX-1 inhibitory function.
source: However, deletion of proline 37 does not impair CPX-1 inhibitory function, indicating that the short AH domain is not an essential feature of nematode complexin structure (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: The worm AH domain comprises a highly stable alpha helix that plays a major role in CPX-mediated inhibition of spontaneous SV fusion.
source: Taken together, these structural and functional results demonstrate that, despite the lack of sequence conservation between worm and mouse AH, the worm AH domain comprises a highly stable alpha helix that plays a major role in CPX-mediated inhibition of spontaneous SV fusion.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined structural and functional data.

claim: Recordings from NMJs of cpx-1 mutants expressing the mouse AH demonstrated that CPX-1 is fully functional with a mouse AH domain.
source: Recordings from the NMJs of cpx-1 mutants expressing the mouse AH demonstrated that CPX-1 is fully functional with a mouse AH domain (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Both mouse AH and mouse AHshort restored near wild-type aldicarb sensitivity.
source: Both mouse AH and mouse AHshort restored near wild-type aldicarb sensitivity, further indicating that the mouse AH is functional in the context of worm CPX-1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The precise length of the AH is not conserved across species.
source: The precise length of the AH is not conserved across species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the spacing between the N-terminal domain and the CH is not likely to play a critical role in CPX-1 function since the NTD can be deleted without significantly impairing CPX-1 inhibitory function in worm (Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The NTD can be deleted without significantly impairing CPX-1 inhibitory function in worm.
source: The precise length of the AH is not conserved across species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the spacing between the N-terminal domain and the CH is not likely to play a critical role in CPX-1 function since the NTD can be deleted without significantly impairing CPX-1 inhibitory function in worm (Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: The AH(h→E) variant with hydrophobic residues replaced by glutamates was fully functional.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, the AH(h→E) was fully functional in the absence of all hydrophobic side chains.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The short mouse AH chimera was functional even when its hydrophobic residues were replaced with glutamates.
source: Moreover, the short mouse AH chimera was also functional even when its hydrophobic residues were replaced with glutamates.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Hydrophobic residues in the AH domain do not play a critical conserved role in complexin function.
source: These findings indicate that hydrophobic residues in the AH domain do not play a critical conserved role in complexin function.
evidence: This is concluded from the functional rescue with hydrophobic-to-glutamate substitutions.

claim: The R43P mutant displayed decreased NMR carbon secondary shifts throughout the AH and extending well into the CH domain.
source: Indeed, decreased NMR carbon secondary shifts were observed throughout the AH and extending well into the CH domain, confirming decreases in both nucleation and propagation of the helical conformation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The R43P variant displayed a lower propensity for helix formation with lower cooperativity.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, the R43P variant displayed a lower propensity for helix formation with a lower cooperativity, consistent with both decreased helix nucleation and propagation, as also evident from both the computational predictions and the NMR data.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Inserting a proline into the AH domain completely eliminated AH function.
source: In living worms, inserting a proline into the AH domain completely eliminated AH function since the CPX(R43P) rescue was indistinguishable from the ΔAHshort rescue in both electrophysiological (Figure 4D,E) and behavioral (Figure 4F) assays of synaptic function.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Inhibition of spontaneous fusion requires a helical AH domain in vivo.
source: Thus, inhibition of spontaneous fusion requires a helical AH domain in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the R43P experiment showing loss of function.

claim: Transgenic animals expressing a series of CPX-1 variants display a level of aldicarb sensitivity that mirrors the helical stability.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, transgenic animals expressing this series of CPX-1 variants display a level of aldicarb sensitivity that mirrors the helical stability (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Insertion of a GG between the AH and CH was equivalent to deleting the entire AH domain.
source: Rescue of cpx-1 mutants with the GG variant demonstrated that insertion of a GG between the AH and CH was equivalent to deleting the entire AH domain (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Helix propagation from the AH domain to the CH domain plays a major role in CPX-1 inhibitory function.
source: Thus helix propagation from the AH domain to the CH domain appears to play a major role in CPX-1 inhibitory function, in agreement with a similar finding at the fly NMJ (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is concluded from the GG insertion experiment with citation to similar findings.

claim: The 7-turn artificial alpha helix provides a stable helical substitute for the endogenous AH domain.
source: Thus, the 7-turn artificial alpha helix provides a stable helical substitute for the endogenous AH domain irrespective of its increased length.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on CD spectroscopy data.

claim: The 7-turn helix fully rescued both aldicarb sensitivity and suppression of spontaneous fusion at cholinergic NMJs.
source: Surprisingly, the 7-turn helix fully rescued both aldicarb sensitivity and suppression of spontaneous fusion at cholinergic NMJs (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: The conserved negative charge density of the AH domain was not essential for CPX inhibition.
source: Moreover, the AH(7-turn) sequence is electrostatically neutral overall, yet it fully restored CPX inhibition. Therefore, the conserved negative charge density of the AH domain was not essential for CPX inhibition.
evidence: This is concluded from the 7-turn rescue experiment which has neutral charge.

claim: The charge density of the rescuing transgenes generally did not correlate with their function in vivo.
source: In fact, the charge density of the rescuing transgenes used in this study generally did not correlate with their function in vivo (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A critical feature of AH function is the nucleation and invasion of a stable alpha helix into the CH domain.
source: Together with the progressive AH destabilizing substitutions and GG insertion, these results reveal that a critical feature of AH function is the nucleation and invasion of a stable alpha helix into the CH domain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The mechanism of AH function is deeply conserved and relatively independent of primary protein sequence, hydrophobicity, length, or net charge density.
source: Our results suggest that the mechanism of AH function is deeply conserved and relatively independent of the primary protein sequence, hydrophobicity, length, or net charge density, inconsistent with models that rely on specific AH-protein interactions or electrostatic AH-membrane interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the results.

claim: CH binding to SNAREs is reduced in the absence of the AH in mouse Cpx1.
source: An appealing model is that a stabilized CH alpha helix interacts more efficiently with the assembling SNARE bundle thereby promoting the SNARE interaction required for complexin inhibition. Indeed, CH binding to SNAREs is reduced in the absence of the AH in mouse Cpx1 (Xue et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation.

claim: The nucleation and propagation function of the AH domain is universal for proper complexin function across species.
source: Nevertheless, our data indicate that the nucleation and propagation function of the AH domain is universal for proper complexin function across species.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: The recombinant worm AH formed a highly stable alpha helix in solution similar to the mouse AH.
source: Further, the recombinant worm AH formed a highly stable alpha helix in solution similar to the mouse AH.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by NMR and CD data in the results.

claim: Abolishing the hydrophobic character of the worm or mouse AH domain had little effect on function.
source: Abolishing the hydrophobic character of the worm or mouse AH domain had little effect, whereas disrupting helix stability and invasion of helical structure into the CH severely impaired complexin inhibitory function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the h→E substitution experiments.

claim: Disrupting helix stability and invasion of helical structure into the CH severely impaired complexin inhibitory function.
source: Abolishing the hydrophobic character of the worm or mouse AH domain had little effect, whereas disrupting helix stability and invasion of helical structure into the CH severely impaired complexin inhibitory function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the R43P and GG insertion experiments.

claim: The 7-turn artificial helix sequence was functional despite large differences in length, charge, and hydrophobicity.
source: Remarkably, this sequence was functional despite large differences in length, charge, and hydrophobicity, indicating that these properties are not critical for AH function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the 7-turn rescue experiment.

claim: Length, charge, and hydrophobicity are not critical for AH function.
source: Remarkably, this sequence was functional despite large differences in length, charge, and hydrophobicity, indicating that these properties are not critical for AH function.
evidence: This is concluded from the 7-turn rescue experiment.

claim: The principal role of the AH domain is to nucleate and propagate helical structure into the CH domain.
source: These experiments indicate that the principal role of the AH domain is to nucleate and propagate helical structure into the CH domain, and this function is conserved across evolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The function of nucleating and propagating helical structure is conserved across evolution.
source: These experiments indicate that the principal role of the AH domain is to nucleate and propagate helical structure into the CH domain, and this function is conserved across evolution.
evidence: This is concluded from the cross-species experiments.

claim: The AH domain of Ta shares 40% identity with the human AH domain.
source: However, whereas the AH domain of Ta shares 40% identity with the human AH domain, there is only 10% sequence conservation between Ml and human AH domains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on sequence analysis.

claim: There is only 10% sequence conservation between Ml and human AH domains.
source: However, whereas the AH domain of Ta shares 40% identity with the human AH domain, there is only 10% sequence conservation between Ml and human AH domains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on sequence analysis.

claim: The CH domains of Ta and Ml share 44% identity with the human Cpx1 CH.
source: Interestingly, the CH domains of these representatives of basal animal phyla, share 44% identity with the human Cpx1 CH.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on sequence analysis.

claim: Ta is predicted to have only a modest degree of stable helical structure on its own.
source: The predicted AH and CH structures for human and Ml both contain extended regions of stable helix propagation similar to worm, whereas Ta is predicted to have only a modest degree of stable helical structure on its own (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The predicted AH and CH structures for human and Ml both contain extended regions of stable helix propagation similar to worm.
source: The predicted AH and CH structures for human and Ml both contain extended regions of stable helix propagation similar to worm, whereas Ta is predicted to have only a modest degree of stable helical structure on its own (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Helical stability is highly dependent on ambient temperature.
source: Helical stability is highly dependent on ambient temperature, so the higher body temperatures of mammals and many other vertebrates may necessitate more stable helical sequences (Privalov, 1982; Scholtz and Baldwin, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: Inhibition by complexin depends on the integrity of its AH domain in all studies where this domain has been examined.
source: Inhibition by complexin depends on the integrity of its AH domain in all studies where this domain has been examined (Xue et al., 2007; Giraudo et al., 2008; Chicka and Chapman, 2009; Giraudo et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2009; Cho et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010; Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kummel et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with multiple citations.

claim: Mutations expected to disrupt the hydrophobic interaction between the AH domain and the tSNAREs did not impair inhibition of spontaneous SV fusion in vivo in fly.
source: A recent study examining the trans Cpx/SNARE array model in the fly NMJ found that mutations expected to disrupt the hydrophobic interaction between the AH domain and the tSNAREs did not impair inhibition of spontaneous SV fusion in vivo (Cho et al., 2014) in agreement with the hydrophobic residue substitutions used in the present study.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation.

claim: The 7-turn construct displayed a lower apparent cooperativity than wild-type CPX-1.
source: Additionally, the 7-turn construct displayed a lower apparent cooperativity than wild-type CPX-1 (2.8 for 7-turn vs 5.6 for wild type), but the true cooperativity of the 7-turn polypeptide was underestimated since it was quite helical even at 0% TFE (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 7-turn polypeptide was quite helical even at 0% TFE.
source: Additionally, the 7-turn construct displayed a lower apparent cooperativity than wild-type CPX-1 (2.8 for 7-turn vs 5.6 for wild type), but the true cooperativity of the 7-turn polypeptide was underestimated since it was quite helical even at 0% TFE (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The EAAK motif creates a strong hydrophobic moment rotated approximately 90° relative to wild-type CPX-1.
source: The EAAK motif also creates a strong hydrophobic moment, but the orientation of the moment is rotated approximately 90° relative to wild-type CPX-1, indicating that AH function is not sensitive to the positioning of the hydrophobic residues (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: AH function is not sensitive to the positioning of the hydrophobic residues.
source: The EAAK motif also creates a strong hydrophobic moment, but the orientation of the moment is rotated approximately 90° relative to wild-type CPX-1, indicating that AH function is not sensitive to the positioning of the hydrophobic residues (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is concluded from the 7-turn rescue with different hydrophobic moment orientation.

claim: The 7-turn variant is more helical than wild type based on CD spectroscopy.
source: CD spectroscopy of TFE titrations on recombinant CPX-1(ΔCT) containing the 7-turn helix revealed that this variant is more helical than wild type (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 7-turn polypeptide forms a more stable helix than wild-type CPX-1 based on helix-coil equilibrium constants.
source: As an independent measure of helical stability, we compared the helix-coil equilibrium constants derived from TFE titrations and found that the 7-turn polypeptide forms a more stable helix than wild-type CPX-1 (17.9% for 7-turn vs 32.4% for wild type).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on CD spectroscopy analysis.

claim: Inserting three glycines produced a similar loss of function as the GG insertion.
source: This disruption is not due to a shift in the orientation of AH domain hydrophobic residues (a consequence of inserting two residues) since inserting three glycines produced a similar loss of function (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: All transgenic rescue experiments utilized a functional CPX-1::GFP fusion protein.
source: All transgenic rescue experiments reported in this study utilized a functional CPX-1::GFP fusion protein, and transgene expression was monitored by imaging neuromuscular junction (NMJ) fluorescence in living intact animals (Martin et al., 2011; Wragg et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the experimental methods.

claim: Transgene expression was monitored by imaging neuromuscular junction fluorescence in living intact animals.
source: All transgenic rescue experiments reported in this study utilized a functional CPX-1::GFP fusion protein, and transgene expression was monitored by imaging neuromuscular junction (NMJ) fluorescence in living intact animals (Martin et al., 2011; Wragg et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the experimental methods.
